title: Resting in the Two Turning Points of the Breath

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret | utpattidvitayasthāne bharaṇād bharitā sthitiḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Bhairava answers: the supreme power, whose nature is to pour itself out (visarga), keeps sounding as the breath: prāṇa moving upward and out, jīva moving downward and in. By filling with awareness the two places where these movements arise, one comes to rest in fullness (bharitā sthitiḥ).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh's notes (following the Kashmir Shaiva commentators) place the two points at the heart-centre, where the in-breath ends, and the outer dvādaśānta, about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose, where the out-breath ends. The verse itself only says 'the two places of arising'.

instruction: Breathe naturally and let awareness rest where the breath turns: inside after the in-breath, outside after the out-breath.

method.text: Breathe naturally. At the end of each in-breath, rest awareness for a moment at the inner turning point; at the end of each out-breath, rest it at the outer turning point. Do not stop, slow or lengthen the breath; meet the pause that is already there.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 24 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. If counting helps, an even four in and four out; otherwise do not count. No forced hold. Notice the natural brief turn at the top and bottom of each breath.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The two places where the breath turns: inside (heart-centre) and outside (space in front of the nose)
attention.secondary: The fullness of the pause itself

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The dharana's own map is two points joined by the path of the breath: the inner point where the in-breath ends and the outer point where the out-breath ends. The exact locations come from commentary (Singh's notes), not from the verse.
points: inner turning point: heart-centre (commentarial)
outer turning point: about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose (commentarial, 'outer dvādaśānta')

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never hold or stop the breath for this door. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

beats.title: Exit / integrate

title: Not Turning Back from the Two Spaces

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (cont.) (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: maruto 'ntar bahir vāpi viyadyugmānivartanāt | bhairavyā bhairavasyetthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ ||
dharana.rendering: O Bhairavī, when the breath, whether it has moved inward or outward, is not hurried back from the two spaces where it comes to rest, the inner and the outer, then in this way Bhairava's form shows itself through Bhairavī.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh describes the two spaces as the split-second pauses at the heart-centre and at the outer dvādaśānta. Singh calls the two pauses the outer and inner kumbhaka but describes them as split-second natural pauses that are only observed; this school follows that observational reading.

instruction: Breathe naturally and stay present in the small space after each in-breath and each out-breath, without hurrying on.

method.text: Breathe naturally. Notice the small space after the in-breath and the small space after the out-breath. Stay present in each space instead of hurrying attention back into the next movement. Do not hold the breath to make the space longer.

seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 25 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Let each pause last exactly as long as it naturally lasts; do not lengthen it on purpose. Never force the pause.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The two spaces where the breath rests, inside and outside
attention.secondary: The habit of rushing into the next breath, noticed and softened

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The verse names a pair of spaces (viyad-yugma), one inside and one outside, where the breath pauses. The practice is to stay in each space a moment longer before attention rushes on.

outer space: where the out-breath rests (commentarial: outer dvādaśānta)

dharana.rendering: When the centre (madhya) opens out, the power that has the form of breath neither goes out nor comes in; as thought-constructs fall away in that middle, the state of Bhairava appears through her.

instruction: Rest awareness in the still centre where the breath is neither going out nor coming in. Recognise the pause; never create it.

title: Lightning Rising Centre by Centre

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y3 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: udgacchantīṃ taḍidrūpāṃ praticakraṃ kramāt kramam | ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭitrayaṃ yāvat tāvad ante mahodayaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Contemplate her rising like lightning, from centre to centre (cakra) in sequence, upward as far as three fists above the head; at the end there is the great dawning (mahodaya).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh identifies the power as kuṇḍalinī and 'three fists' as the dvādaśānta. Singh contrasts it with verse 28: here the power climbs through the centres one by one, whereas in verse 28 it goes straight up.

instruction: Gently mark attention centre by centre up the central line, then rest in the space above the crown for a breath or two.

method.text: Gentle form: quietly mark attention centre by centre up the central line (base, belly, heart, throat, brow, crown), then rest awareness in the space above the crown for a breath or two. Contemplative tracing only; never try to produce rushes, heat or shaking, and never force sensation or breath.

breath.cue: Ordinary breath, about four in and six out if counting helps. No forced hold. Never use the breath to drive the image.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: Attention moving centre by centre up the central line to a point above the head
attention.secondary: Resting in the open space at the end

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a vertical line with stations along it, and a quick flash of light passing station by station to a point about three fists above the head.
points: successive centres (cakras) along the central line
three fists above the crown (Singh: dvādaśānta)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Twelve Stations, Twelve Letters

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y4 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kramadvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣarabheditam | sthūlasūkṣmaparasthityā muktvā muktvāntataḥ śivaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Twelve stations in sequence, each properly marked by one of twelve letters: attend to each in its gross, then subtle, then supreme form, leaving each behind in turn; in the end there is Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh's notes list the twelve stations (janmāgra at the level of the generative organ, mūla, kanda, nābhi, hṛd, kaṇṭha, tālu, bhrūmadhya, lalāṭa, brahmarandhra, śakti, vyāpinī) and pair them with twelve vowels (a ā i ī u ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ). The verse itself names neither the stations nor the letters: both lists are commentary.

instruction: Move attention up the centre line one station at a time: feel it coarsely, then subtly, then let it go and rise.

method.text: Classical method (Singh's notes): twelve stations from janmāgra to vyāpinī, linked with the twelve vowels, each contemplated in gross, subtle and supreme phases and then left behind. School simplification (flagged): move attention up a short midline sequence (pelvic floor, navel, heart, throat, brow, crown). At each station feel the coarse sense, then a subtler quiet, then leave it and rise. No phoneme placement, no forced breath-hold.

seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 30 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Equal inhale four, exhale four if counting helps. Keep the breath quiet and even. No forced retention.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One station at a time: feel it coarsely, then subtly, then let it go and rise
attention.secondary: The release itself, each time a station is left

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a ladder of twelve stations, each paired with a letter, climbed and released one at a time through gross, subtle and supreme phases.
points: twelve stations in rising sequence (locations given in commentary, not in the verse)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

instruction: Feel the whole field of the senses as nested rings and let the detail dissolve toward a quiet centre at the heart.

dharana.rendering: In the same graded way, wherever attention rests, whether on empty space, on a wall, or on a worthy vessel, it dissolves there by itself and grants the boon.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: 'pare pātre' is read differently: Singh 'some excellent person' (glossed as a pure-minded, competent pupil), Bäumer 'a worthy disciple', Chaudhri 'a great person', Silburn 'receptacle suprême', Wallis 'a perfect vessel'. Singh and S. P. Singh & Maheshvarananda tie 'in this same way' back to the twelve stations of verse 30.

instruction: Rest a soft gaze on empty sky or a blank wall and let attention dissolve into it, blinking whenever needed.

method.text: Rest a soft gaze on empty sky or a blank wall, keep attention there without chasing thoughts, and let it dissolve into the support. dharana.rendering: Remaining with eyes closed, place the mind inside the skull; as steadiness of mind gradually grows, one perceives the highest thing to be perceived.

instruction: Close the eyes and rest attention inside the skull as a soft field, letting steadiness build without force.

title: Bathing in the Unstruck Sound

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y12 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.hatha_es: dharana 15 = a variant of verse 42 (piṇḍa-mantra fading into void); non-standard, not followed (the previous draft of this door followed it)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: anāhate pātrakarṇe 'bhagnaśabde sariddrute | śabdabrahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati ||
dharana.rendering: One who is steeped in sound-Brahman, the unstruck (anāhata) and unbroken sound that rushes like a river and is heard by the fit ear, reaches the supreme Brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: niṣṇāta means both 'well-versed' and 'bathed in'; the sound is an inner sound heard by an ear made competent by yoga. Bäumer compares the sound to a waterfall, and Chaudhri adds 'the continuous sound of a river flowing, or by closing the ears' (both as printed in The Mystery Within). The verse itself names neither a waterfall nor closing the ears.

instruction: Listen past ordinary sounds to the subtle, continuous hum of a quiet room and bathe in that unbroken sound.

method.text: Begin with a steady natural sound if helpful (running water, wind, a fan), then let attention move to the subtle continuous hum heard when the room is quiet. Stay immersed in that unbroken sound like bathing in a river. If covering the ears, rest the palms lightly over them without pressing.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 38 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural, quiet breath, about four in and six out if counting helps. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A steady, unbroken stream of sound, followed from outer to inner
attention.secondary: Being immersed in it rather than analysing it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a continuous stream of sound flowing through the vessel of the ear, followed inward until the listener is immersed in it.
points: the ears as a vessel (pātra-karṇa)
a continuous inner stream of sound

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If listening inward makes a ringing or other sound in the ears feel distressing, stop and listen to ordinary sounds in the room instead. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Praṇava Fading into Void

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y13 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: praṇavādisamuccārāt plutānte śūnyabhāvanāt | śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi ||
dharana.rendering: O Bhairavī, by fully sounding the praṇava (such as Oṃ) and contemplating emptiness at the end of its prolonged (pluta) sound, one reaches emptiness through the supreme power that is emptiness.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Lakshmanjoo (via the Lakshmanjoo Academy) names three praṇavas, Oṃ, Hūṃ and Hrīṃ, sounded long with attention resting where the sound dissolves. Singh's note gives the same three (Vedic Auṃ, Śaiva Hūṃ, Śākta Hrīṃ) and stresses that at the end of the protracted sound one contemplates the void, not the usual ardhacandra, bindu and other subtle phases.

instruction: Sound a soft, long Oṃ, aloud or silently, and rest in the quiet gap when the sound ends.

method.text: Sound a soft, drawn-out Oṃ (or another seed-syllable you have been taught), or sound it silently. At the moment the sound ends, rest in the quiet gap. Do not chase the next thought. Do not force breath retention or strain to lengthen the sound.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 39 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Inhale easily. Let the out-breath carry a long, soft Oṃ (or hum it silently) only as long as is comfortable, then rest in the quiet before the next easy in-breath. No forced hold and no straining to make the sound longer.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The moment the sound ends, and the silence after it
attention.secondary: Not reaching for the next thought or the next sound

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one long sound tapering to nothing, and the open silence after it.
points: the sounded syllable
its prolonged tail
the silence after it

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep the sound soft and stop before the breath feels short. If you feel light-headed, return to ordinary breathing. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
